Question 1

What is the trace in the yz-plane of the hyperbolic cylinder (x−4)22−(y+1)27=1?

a
The line y=−1
b
The hyperbola (y+1)27−z2=1
c
The line y=6
d
The ellipse (y+1)27+z22=1
e
The lines y=−8 and y=6

decision.explanation: In the yz-plane, x=0. Substitution gives 8-(y+1)^2/7=1, so (y+1)^2=49 and y=-8 or y=6. Since z is unrestricted, the trace consists of two lines.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: What is the trace in the $yz$-plane of the hyperbolic cylinder $\frac{(x-4)^{2}}{2}-\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{7}=1?$
after.worked_solution:
To find the trace in the $yz$-plane, we substitute $x=0$ into the equation of the cylinder, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(0-4)^{2}}{2}-\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{7} & =1 \\ 8-\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{7} & =1 \\ \frac{(y+1)^{2}}{7} & =7 \\ (y+1)^{2} & =49 \\ y+1 & =\pm 7 \\ y & =-1\pm 7 \\ y & =-8,6\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of two lines $y=-8$ and $y=6$ in the $yz$-plane.

decision.explanation: In the xz-plane, y=0. Substitution gives (x-4)^2/8+1/2=1, so (x-4)^2=4 and x=2 or x=6. Since z is unrestricted, the trace consists of two lines.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: What is the trace in the $xz$-plane of the elliptic cylinder $\frac{(x-4)^{2}}{8}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{2}=1?$
after.worked_solution:
To find the trace in the $xz$-plane, we substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the cylinder, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-4)^{2}}{8}+\frac{(0-1)^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-4)^{2}}{8}+\frac{1}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-4)^{2}}{8} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ (x-4)^{2} & =4 \\ x-4 & =\pm 2 \\ x & =4\pm 2 \\ x & =2,6\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of two lines $x=2$ and $x=6$ in the $xz$-plane.

after.problem: The projection of the intersection between the parabolic cylinder $4(x-3)^{2}=12(z+1)$ and the plane $y=2$ onto the $xz$-plane is a parabola. What is the vertex of the parabola?
after.worked_solution:
To find the intersection of the cylinder and the plane $y=2,$ we substitute $y=2$ into the equation of the cylinder. However, since the equation has no (explicit) $y$ term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4(x-3)^{2} & =12(z+1) \\ (x-3)^{2} & =3(z+1) \\ (x-3)^{2} & =4\cdot \frac{3}{4}\cdot (z+1).\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of a parabola in the $xz$-plane with the vertex at $(3,-1).$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: What is the domain in the $xy$-plane of the hyperbolic cylinder $\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{4}=1?$
after.worked_solution:
The full expression describing all points on our hyperbolic cylinder is

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{4}=1,\,z=k
$$

where $k\in R$ can vary arbitrarily. 

The domain of any cylinder in the $xy$-plane is its base curve. Hence, in this case, the domain is

$$
{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:\text{ }\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{4}=1}.
$$

content.problem: What is the domain in the $xy$-plane of the hyperbolic cylinder $(x-3)^{2}-\frac{(y+6)^{2}}{8}=1?$
content.worked_solution:
The full expression describing all points on our hyperbolic cylinder is

$$
(x-3)^{2}-\frac{(y+6)^{2}}{8}=1,\,z=k
$$

where $k\in R$ can vary arbitrarily. 

The domain of any cylinder in the $xy$-plane is its base curve. Hence, in this case, the domain is

$$
{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:\text{ }(x-3)^{2}-\frac{(y+6)^{2}}{8}=1}.
$$

This is a hyperbola centered at $(3,-6).$
